subject: Science
source: National Curriculum KS1 Science (Living things and their habitats); Drive Science folder 'Science lower school' (3.8 organisms, 3.9 eco-systems) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 2 curriculum map and Science Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Muck, Mess & Mixtures and Will It Degrade?), TGA Year 2 Curriculum Pack (Topic); home practicals with household items | Summer 1 2027 (lessons 10, 11): TGA Year 2 pack, Topic, How Do Germs Spread? (glitter or flour model; handwashing test)

lessons.title: Living, dead and never alive
objectives: Sort things into living, dead and never been alive
Use the seven life processes in simple words
Explain why a thing is living or not

keywords.def: alive now: it moves, feeds, grows and reproduces
once alive but no longer alive
something that has never been alive, like a rock
to have young or make new plants

starter: Bismillah. Name one living thing in a garden.
Name one thing that is not alive.
What do animals and plants need to stay alive?

teach.heading: What does living mean?
teach.note: Teach the life processes in child-friendly words: move, breathe, feed, grow, reproduce, sense, get rid of waste. Plants move by growing and turning towards light. Do not overload; use three at first.

teach.heading: Dead things
teach.note: Show a dry leaf, a feather, a piece of wood. They were once alive. Misconception: a fallen leaf is a living thing; explain it is dead.

teach.heading: Things never alive
bullets: A toy car is not living
teach.note: A pencil is made from wood but is made into an object; keep simple: it is not alive. Ask 'Does a rock need food?'

teach.heading: Sorting game
teach.note: Safe online activity: children bring three household objects (spoon, leaf, toy) and sort into three groups. Check each decision with the question 'Does it need food and water?'

practice: Is a dandelion living, dead or never alive?
Is a stone living, dead or never alive? Explain.
A wooden table was made from a tree. Is the table living, dead or never alive?
independent: Draw a three-column table: living, dead, never alive. Put five things in the columns.
Write one sentence: 'A cat is living because ...'
exit: Give an example of a living thing.
Is a pebble living, dead or never alive?
lessons.homework: Find three things in your home that are living, dead or never alive. Draw them and label them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture cards for sorting and sentence starters 'It is ... because ...'. Stretch: explain why a seed is living even though it does not seem to move.

lessons.title: Habitats
objectives: Match animals and plants to their habitats
Explain why a habitat suits the living things in it

keywords.def: the place where a plant or animal lives
the surroundings of a living thing
a place that keeps an animal safe or protected
a very dry habitat with little water

starter: Bismillah. Is a spider living, dead or never alive?
Where does a fish live? Where does a bird live?
What do all living things need?

teach.heading: What is a habitat?
teach.note: Habitat = natural home of a plant or animal. Ask 'Where do you live?' then 'Where does a fox live?'

teach.heading: Different habitats
teach.note: Show photos of ocean, woodland, desert and pond. Link to camels in desert (children may know camels from family countries). Ask what makes each habitat different (water, shade, temperature).

teach.heading: Why the match works
bullets: A camel stores fat in its hump
A fish has gills and fins
A polar bear has thick fur
teach.note: Camel humps store fat, not water: a common misconception. Explain that the animal's body helps it live in its habitat.

teach.heading: Looking after habitats
bullets: Allah made us carers of the Earth
teach.note: Keep Islamic ethos natural: we are trusted to look after Allah's creation. Ask 'What can you do?' (put litter in a bin, save water).

practice: Which habitat is best for a fish: a pond or a desert?
Why does a camel live well in the desert?
Match: owl, crab, lizard. Habitats: woodland, seashore, desert.
independent: Draw one habitat and two living things that live there. Label them.
Write: 'A ... lives in a ... because it has ...'
exit: Name one animal and the habitat it lives in.
lessons.homework: Choose one animal. Find out where it lives and draw its habitat.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a habitat picture matching sheet with key words. Stretch: explain why a polar bear could not live in the desert.

lessons.title: Microhabitats
objectives: Name small animals that live in microhabitats
Explain why they choose damp, dark places

keywords.def: a very small habitat, like under a stone
a small animal such as a worm, snail or woodlouse
slightly wet
looking carefully to see and count what is there

starter: Name a habitat and an animal that lives in it.
What do living things need from their habitat?

teach.heading: Tiny habitats
bullets: Under a log is a microhabitat
teach.note: Show photos of a log pile and a leaf litter. The smaller the home, the smaller the animals.

teach.heading: Minibeasts
teach.note: Show photos. Why damp? Woodlice breathe through gill-like structures and dry out. Keep language simple: 'they like it damp and dark'.

teach.heading: Safe minibeast hunt
teach.note: Safe online practical: children with a grown-up look under a flowerpot or log in a garden, or you show a short video of a minibeast hunt. Look only; never pick up animals. Wash hands with soap after. Cleanliness is part of faith (hadith in Sahih Muslim: cleanliness is half of faith).

teach.heading: Recording what we find
teach.note: Model a tally chart with 5-bar gates for snails, worms, woodlice. Practise tallying to 8 together.

practice: Where might you find a woodlouse: under a stone or on a sunny wall?
Why do small animals like damp places?
independent: Draw a tally chart for woodlice (4), snails (3), worms (5) and fill it in.
Draw a microhabitat under a log and label two animals.
lessons.homework: With a grown-up, look carefully in a garden or park for a microhabitat. Draw one minibeast you see. Wash your hands.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a picture tally sheet. Stretch: compare two microhabitats and say which has more minibeasts and why.

lessons.title: Simple food chains
objectives: Say that all animals need food
Build and explain a simple food chain with arrows

keywords.def: a line showing what eats what
a plant that makes its own food
an animal that hunts and eats other animals
an animal that is hunted and eaten

starter: Name a minibeast and its home.
Where do animals get their food from?

teach.heading: Where food comes from
teach.note: Ask 'Who eats grass?' (rabbit, cow). Say 'plants use sunlight to make their own food' without detail. Energy begins with the Sun.

teach.heading: A food chain
teach.note: Draw: grass -> rabbit -> fox. Read it aloud: 'The grass is eaten by the rabbit.' Misconception: arrows mean 'goes to'. Stress 'is eaten by'.

teach.heading: Predator and prey
bullets: Prey can be a plant eater
teach.note: Predator hunts; prey is hunted. Many animals can be both: a small bird eats insects and is eaten by a hawk.

teach.heading: Pond chain
teach.note: Model another chain so children see the pattern: plant first. Ask children to suggest the last link.

practice: Which one is the predator: rabbit or fox?
Read this chain aloud: leaf -> caterpillar -> bird.
independent: Draw a food chain with three living things and arrows. Label the producer.
Write two sentences about your chain using 'is eaten by'.
exit: What does the arrow in a food chain mean?
lessons.homework: Make a food chain for a garden using three animals or plants you know. Draw and label it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use cut-out pictures to arrange the chain. Stretch: build a four-link chain and name the predator and prey.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials and how they change (Muck, Mess & Mixtures and Will It Degrade?)
lessons.title: What are everyday materials?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are spoons not made of paper?
objectives: To understand that everyday objects are made from different materials for a reason
successCriteria: All: name five materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper
Most: sort objects by the material they are made from
Some: say why an object is made from its material
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: thanking Allah for the materials we use

keywords.def: what an object is made of
a thing you can touch
a thin material made from wood
a hard, see-through material
a material made in factories that can be shaped

hook.text: Look around your room. Which material can you see the most of?

islamicLink.text: Allah created the trees, the sand and the metals in the earth, and people make useful things from them: wood from trees, glass from sand, paper from wood. Allah says He sent down iron with great strength and many benefits for people (al-Hadid 57:25).

starter.q: Which season is January in?
Is a window transparent or opaque?
Name one thing made of wood.
starter.a: For example: a table, a door, a pencil

teach.heading: Five everyday materials
teach.note: Hold up a pencil: wood outside, graphite inside. Ask pupils to hold up something made of plastic.

teach.heading: Sort them
teach.note: Pupils say the letter and the group. Discuss any that use two materials.

teach.heading: Why that material?
bullets: Spoons are metal: hard and strong
Books are paper: light and easy to write on
teach.note: Ask: what would happen to a paper spoon in hot soup? It would go soggy and tear.

misconception.wrong: All objects of one kind are made of the same material
misconception.right: A cup can be glass, plastic, metal or china: we choose the best one for the job

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which object is usually made of paper?
check.why: Books are paper. Keys are metal and windows are glass.

practice.q: What is a coin made of?
practice.model:
It is hard, cold and shiny.
Those are clues for metal.
A coin is made of metal.

practice.q: What is a jar often made of?
Name an object made of two materials.
practice.a: For example: a pencil (wood and graphite), scissors (metal and plastic)

independent.q: Core: Material hunt in the kitchen: find one object made of each of wood, metal, plastic, glass and paper. Show each one.
independent.a: For example: wooden spoon, metal fork, plastic tub, glass jar, paper bag
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: this is a paper bag. It is thin and folds. It is paper.

independent.q: Extend: Choose one object and say why it is made of that material.
independent.a: For example: a fork is metal because metal is strong and hard

independent.q: Stretch: Name a material that is natural and one made by people.
independent.a: Natural: wood or stone; made by people: plastic or glass

exit.q: A plastic tub is made of plastic:
Big question: why are spoons not made of paper?
exit.a: Paper is weak and soaks up water, so it would tear and go soggy

lessons.homework: Find five objects at home and draw each one with the name of its material.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects to hold and five material cards. EAL: 'It is made of ...' sentence starter. Stretch: find objects made from three materials.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials and how they change (Muck, Mess & Mixtures and Will It Degrade?)
lessons.title: Testing properties with kitchen items
lessons.bigQuestion: Which material would make the best dishcloth?
objectives: To understand how simple tests show the properties of materials
successCriteria: All: say if a material is hard or soft
Most: test which materials are absorbent or waterproof
Some: use test results to choose a material for a job
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: recording results in a table
lessons.smsc: Moral: not wasting water during the test

keywords.def: what a material is like
soaks up water
does not let water through
bends without breaking
stiff, does not bend

hook.text: Why do we dry our hands on a towel and not on a plastic bag?

starter.q: A key is made of:
Glass is made from:
Name one object made of plastic.
starter.a: For example: a bottle, a tub, a toy

teach.heading: Properties
teach.note: Show a sponge, a spoon, a rubber band and foil. Ask pupils to describe each with one word.

teach.heading: The drip test
bullets: Drip 3 spoons of water on each
Does it soak in or run off?
teach.note: Model on a tray: kitchen roll soaks it up; foil does not.

teach.heading: The bend and stretch test
teach.note: A rubber band stretches; a wooden spoon is rigid; foil is flexible but not stretchy.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which is the best dishcloth material?
check.why: A sponge is absorbent so it soaks up water. Foil and plastic are waterproof.

practice.q: Is kitchen roll absorbent or waterproof?
practice.model:
Drip water on it.
The water soaks in and spreads.
So it is absorbent.

practice.q: Is a wooden spoon flexible or rigid?
Which is stretchy: a rubber band or foil?

independent.q: Core: Test four kitchen items (kitchen roll, foil, a sponge, a plastic bag) with the drip test. Record soaks in or runs off.
independent.a: Kitchen roll: soaks in; foil: runs off; sponge: soaks in; plastic bag: runs off
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 3 spoons of water on the sponge, watch, it soaks in, write 'absorbent'.

independent.q: Extend: Which item was best for mopping a spill?
independent.a: The sponge or kitchen roll, because they are absorbent

independent.q: Stretch: Which would you use to wrap a sandwich to keep it dry?
independent.a: Foil, because it is waterproof

exit.q: Big question: which material would make the best dishcloth?
exit.a: An absorbent one, such as a sponge or cotton cloth

lessons.homework: Find one absorbent and one waterproof object at home and tell an adult how you know.
lessons.send: SEND: adult drips the water; tick cards for soaks in or runs off. EAL: soak, drip, stretch with actions. Stretch: test a fifth material and predict first.

Results table: four materials (portal printable)
Kitchen roll, foil, a sponge, a plastic bag (adult only, away from faces), a rubber band, a teaspoon, water, a tray

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials and how they change (Muck, Mess & Mixtures and Will It Degrade?)
lessons.title: Squash, bend, stretch and twist
lessons.bigQuestion: Can you change the shape of a material without breaking it?
objectives: To understand that some materials change shape when we squash, bend, stretch or twist them
successCriteria: All: name the four actions: squash, bend, stretch, twist
Most: say which materials change shape and which do not
Some: say whether the shape stays changed or goes back
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: choosing materials that can be shaped
lessons.smsc: Social: sharing equipment and tidying up afterwards

keywords.def: press hard to make flatter
make into a curve
pull to make longer
turn the ends different ways
a push or a pull

hook.text: What happens to play dough if you sit on it? What happens to a ball?

starter.q: A sponge is:
Is a wooden spoon rigid or flexible?
Name one stretchy material.
starter.a: For example: a rubber band, a sock

teach.heading: Four actions
teach.note: Do each action with your hands as pupils copy. Each one uses a force: a push or a pull.

teach.heading: Try it
bullets: A sponge squashes then springs back
teach.note: Model with dough, sponge, foil. Ask: did it go back to its shape?

teach.heading: Some materials do not change
bullets: A metal spoon will not squash by hand
Glass must never be bent: it breaks
teach.note: Ask: why are bridges made of materials that do not bend easily?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which goes back to its shape after squashing?
check.why: A sponge springs back. Dough and foil stay squashed.

practice.q: Which action makes a rubber band longer?
practice.model:
I hold both ends.
I pull them apart.
It gets longer.
That is stretching.

practice.q: What happens to dough when you squash it?
practice.a: It gets flatter and stays flat

practice.q: Which action do we use to wring out a cloth?

independent.q: Core: Squash, bend, stretch and twist dough, foil and a sponge. Record what changed.
independent.a: Dough: all actions change it and it stays changed; foil: bends and twists and stays; sponge: squashes and springs back
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: twist the dough. It changes shape and stays twisted. Write 'twist: stays'.

independent.q: Extend: Which material went back to its shape?
independent.a: The sponge

independent.q: Stretch: Why are car tyres made of rubber that springs back?
independent.a: So they can squash on bumps and go back to shape

exit.q: Big question: can you change the shape of a material without breaking it?
exit.a: Yes: dough, foil and sponge change shape when we squash, bend, stretch or twist them

lessons.homework: Make a shape from foil by bending and twisting it; show it next lesson and say which actions you used.
lessons.send: SEND: action cards with pictures. EAL: squash, bend, stretch, twist with actions. Stretch: sort materials into 'stays changed' and 'springs back'.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 2 curriculum map and long-term plans 2023-24; TGA Year 2 Curriculum Pack, Topic, Spring 1 Muck, Mess & Mixtures (Cornerstones Maestro: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Home practical guide: changing shape (portal worksheet)
Play dough (or salt dough: flour, salt, water), foil, a sponge, a rubber band
Changing shape record sheet (portal printable)
Mini-whiteboard and pen

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials and how they change (Muck, Mess & Mixtures and Will It Degrade?)
lessons.title: Will it degrade? Setting up a soil test
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to rubbish when it is buried in soil?
objectives: To understand how to set up a fair test to see which materials degrade in soil
successCriteria: All: say what degrade means
Most: predict which materials will degrade
Some: say how the test is kept fair
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: same amounts of soil and water
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the earth by wasting less

keywords.def: break down into tiny bits over time
go soft and break down
rotted plant waste that feeds soil
say what you think will happen
a test where only one thing changes

hook.text: Where does a fallen leaf go in the end?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the earth so that dead leaves and peel break down and feed new plants. Allah tells us that we were created from the earth and will return to it (Ta Ha 20:55). Allah made us caretakers of the earth, so we should not fill it with rubbish that never rots.

starter.q: Which action makes a rubber band longer?
Is a banana peel natural or made by people?
Name one material made by people.

teach.heading: What does degrade mean?
bullets: Some things break down in soil
Tiny living things help them rot
They become part of the soil
teach.note: Leaves, peel and paper rot. Worms and tiny living things called microbes break them down.

teach.heading: Our test
teach.note: Bury each item the same depth. Label each jar. Keep jars in the same place.

teach.heading: Keep it fair and safe
bullets: Wash hands; do not open old food
teach.note: Safety: an adult helps; wear gloves if you have them; wash hands after touching soil.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which do you predict will rot first?
check.why: Peel is natural and soft, so microbes break it down quickly. Plastic and metal do not rot in a week.

practice.model:
Peel is part of a plant.
Plants rot in soil.
So I predict it will degrade quickly.

practice.q: Predict: will a plastic bag degrade?
practice.a: No, not for a very long time

practice.q: Why do we use the same soil in every jar?

independent.q: Core: With an adult, set up four jars (peel, paper, plastic, cloth). Label them and write your prediction for each.
independent.a: Peel: rots fast; paper: rots slowly; cotton cloth: rots slowly; plastic: does not rot
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: soil in the jar, peel in the middle, more soil on top, two spoons of water, label 'peel: I think it will rot'.

independent.q: Extend: Why do you think plastic does not rot?
independent.a: It is made by people and microbes cannot break it down easily

independent.q: Stretch: How could this help us look after the earth?
independent.a: Use less plastic and compost food peel

exit.q: Big question: what happens to rubbish when it is buried in soil?
exit.a: Natural things like peel rot away; plastic stays for a very long time

lessons.homework: Put your jars somewhere safe, keep the soil damp and draw what you see on day 3.
lessons.send: SEND: adult sets up the jars while the pupil labels with picture cards. EAL: rot, soil, predict with pictures. Stretch: add a fifth jar with a leaf.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 2 curriculum map and long-term plans 2023-24; TGA Year 2 Curriculum Pack, Topic, Spring 1 Muck, Mess & Mixtures (Cornerstones Maestro: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Home practical guide and safety card: Will It Degrade? soil jars (portal worksheet): adult helps, gloves if available, wash hands
Four clear jars or cut plastic bottles (adult cuts), garden soil, water, labels
Banana peel, a strip of paper, a piece of plastic bag, a piece of old cotton cloth
Prediction sheet (portal printable)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials and how they change (Muck, Mess & Mixtures and Will It Degrade?)
lessons.title: Will it degrade? Our results
lessons.bigQuestion: Which materials go back to the earth, and which stay?
objectives: To understand how to use results to draw a simple conclusion
successCriteria: All: say what happened to each material
Most: compare the results with our predictions
Some: give a reason why the results came out that way
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: litter on coasts and in the sea
lessons.smsc: Moral: our duty to care for Allah's earth

keywords.def: what happened in a test
say what is the same and different
what we found out
say how good our test was
break down into tiny bits over time

hook.text: If you buried a crisp packet today, would it still be there when you are a grown-up?

islamicLink.text: Allah made us caretakers of the earth. Allah says that corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have done (ar-Rum 30:41). Our test shows that plastic stays in the earth, so we use less of it, reuse it and put rubbish in the right place.

starter.q: Degrade means:
Which material did we predict would rot first?
Why did we use the same soil?

teach.heading: Look, do not dig
teach.note: Safety first: look through the side of the jar. If the peel is mouldy, an adult puts the jar outside.

teach.heading: Typical results after one week
bullets: Peel: soft, brown, starting to rot
teach.note: Results after one week are small. Peel changes most. Real composting takes weeks and months.

teach.heading: Our conclusion
bullets: Some take longer than a week
teach.note: Model the sentence: I found out that ... because ...

steps: Say what happened: the peel rotted most
Say what did not change: the plastic
Say why: microbes break down natural things
model.answer: I found out that peel degrades quickly but plastic does not, because microbes break down natural materials.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: What does our test show about plastic?
check.why: Plastic showed no change; it can last for hundreds of years.

practice.a: It went brown and soft: it started to rot
practice.model:
Look at the jar.
The peel is brown and soft.
It has started to rot.

practice.q: Was your prediction about plastic right?
Which changed more, paper or cloth?

independent.q: Core: Draw your four jars and write one word under each: rotting, soggy, same, no change.
independent.a: Peel: rotting; paper: soggy; cloth: same; plastic: no change
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I draw the peel jar. The peel is brown. I write 'rotting'.

independent.q: Extend: Write your conclusion: 'I found out that ... because ...'
independent.a: I found out that peel degrades but plastic does not, because tiny living things break down natural materials

independent.q: Stretch: How could we make the test better?
independent.a: For example: leave it longer or use the same size pieces

exit.q: Big question: which materials go back to the earth, and which stay?
exit.a: Natural ones like peel and paper go back; plastic stays for a very long time

lessons.homework: Keep watching your jars over the break and draw them again in two weeks: what has changed?
lessons.send: SEND: picture word mat with rotting, soggy, same. EAL: conclusion frame 'I found out that ...'. Stretch: explain why litter on beaches harms animals.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Germs and handwashing (How Do Germs Spread?)
lessons.title: What are germs and how do they spread?
lessons.bigQuestion: If germs are too small to see, how can we tell where they have been?
objectives: To understand what germs are and how they spread from person to person
successCriteria: All: say what a germ is
Most: name two ways germs spread
Some: explain what the glitter test shows

keywords.def: a tiny living thing that can make us ill
move from one place to more places
keeping clean to stay healthy
something we use to show an idea
air bursting out of your nose and mouth

hook.text: Where in your home do you think the most germs are hiding?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ taught that purity is half of faith (Muslim). Keeping clean is part of being a Muslim, and it also protects other people from germs.

starter.q: North on a map is at the:
A key tells you what the ... mean.
Name a material that is waterproof.

teach.heading: Tiny living things
bullets: Germs are too small to see
Colds and tummy bugs come from germs
teach.note: Not all tiny living things are bad, but some germs make us poorly.

teach.heading: How germs spread
teach.note: Catch it, bin it, wash your hands.

teach.heading: Glitter test
bullets: Put a little on one hand
Touch things and see it spread
teach.note: Model on camera: glitter on palm, touch a cup and a book; show where it went. Adult helps; flour works too.

steps: Pinch of glitter on one palm
Touch a cup, a book and a spoon
model.answer: Glitter is on all three: germs spread by touch

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Catch the sneeze in a tissue, put it in the bin, then wash hands to kill the germs.

practice.q: Can we see germs with our eyes?
practice.model:
Germs are tiny.
They are smaller than a speck of dust.
We cannot see them.
So we use glitter as a model.

practice.a: Touch, coughs, sneezes, dirty food or water

independent.q: Core: Do the glitter (or flour) test with an adult. Record which objects got glitter on them.
independent.a: A record showing glitter on every object touched
independent.model: Teacher shows the record table from the model test.

independent.q: Extend: Write how glitter is like germs.
independent.a: It spreads to everything we touch, like germs do

independent.q: Stretch: How is the model different from real germs?
independent.a: Glitter can be seen; real germs cannot

exit.q: Big question: how can we tell where germs have been?
exit.a: Use a model like glitter to show how they spread by touch

lessons.homework: Keep the glitter on a paper plate and tell your family how germs spread by touch.
lessons.send: SEND: picture record sheet. EAL: germ, spread, sneeze with pictures. Stretch: suggest where germs spread most at home and why.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Germs and handwashing (How Do Germs Spread?)
lessons.title: Washing hands: water only or soap and water?
lessons.bigQuestion: Is water on its own enough to clean your hands?
objectives: To understand why washing with soap and water removes germs better than water alone
successCriteria: All: carry out the glitter washing test
Most: compare water only with soap and water
Some: link handwashing to wudu
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: wudu and keeping clean
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: cleanliness as part of faith

keywords.def: it helps lift dirt and germs off skin
only one thing changes
say what is the same and what is different
washing before prayer
free from dirt and germs

hook.text: Why do you think doctors wash their hands so carefully?

islamicLink.text: Allah says He loves those who turn to Him and those who keep themselves pure (Al-Baqarah 2:222). Muslims wash in wudu before every prayer, so keeping hands clean is part of our worship and our health.

starter.q: Germs are:
In the glitter test, glitter stood for:
Name one way germs spread.

teach.heading: Our question
bullets: Water only, or soap and water?
teach.note: We change only one thing: soap or no soap. Everything else stays the same.

teach.heading: A fair test
teach.note: Count 20 seconds aloud together (no songs).

teach.heading: How to wash
teach.note: Model the wash on camera.

model.answer: Most of the glitter is gone

teach.heading: Clean for prayer
bullets: Wudu washes hands, face, arms and feet
Allah loves those who keep clean
teach.note: Allah loves those who purify themselves (Al-Baqarah 2:222).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Soap lifts the glitter and germs off the skin; water alone leaves more behind.

practice.q: What is the one thing we change?
practice.model:
In a fair test only one thing changes.
We keep the glitter and time the same.
We change the soap.

practice.q: How long do we rub our hands?

independent.q: Core: With an adult, do the test: glitter on, wash with water only for 20 seconds, look; glitter on again, wash with soap and water for 20 seconds, look. Record a lot, some or none left.
independent.a: Water only: some or a lot left; soap and water: little or none left
independent.model: Teacher shows the results table from the model test.

independent.q: Extend: Write a sentence: 'Soap and water is better because...'
independent.a: ...it removes more glitter, so it removes more germs

independent.q: Stretch: When should we wash our hands?
independent.a: Before eating, after the toilet, after sneezing, before wudu

exit.q: We should rub hands with soap for:
Big question: is water on its own enough?
exit.a: No, soap and water removes more germs

lessons.homework: Teach someone at home how to wash hands for 20 seconds with soap. Germs quiz next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: picture steps for washing. EAL: soap, wash, rinse, dry with gestures. Stretch: plan a test with warm and cold water.
